Copper's been thin for five weeks. Haven't told Ainsley. Haven't told anyone.

Ainsley knows. Of course she knows. She's always known everything before I find the words.

I look at the floor between us. The 400 sim she's holding - that's the debt to Marta, the money I borrowed for the assay on a seam that came up empty. Ainsley's been carrying that weight in silence, same as me. And now she's telling me to walk past Marta's door for a loaf, knowing I owe her more than I can pay.

"Tell her I'll settle it before harvest." Before harvest. She knows the seam is running thin too, even if I haven't said it. Twenty years married, and she hears what I don't speak.

I can't look at her directly when I answer. The dignity of silence, I always thought. But silence isn't dignity. It's just fear wearing a better coat. </think>  "We'll see." I meant no. I always mean no when I say we'll see.

But I need that loaf. The seam is thin, but I can't work a thin seam on an empty belly. And walking past Marta's door without the 400 sim in my hand - that's a weight I don't know how to carry.

Twenty years married, and I still can't say the numbers out loud. Ainsley knows. She always knows.

I need to move. Either to Marta's for that bread, or straight to the outcrop and hope the copper runs better than it has. But standing here between two women who've already seen through me - that's a seam I can't read.

I look at the door.

Nell's voice cuts through the room like a pick through soft rock. She sees it—the silence, the weight, the thing we've been carrying between us without naming it. Paid off one man's silence, she says. Her husband's, maybe. The father who died owing, or the debt that outlived him.

I feel the old pressure in my throat. The words are there—400 sim, thin seam, empty assay—but they won't come out. Twenty years of not saying numbers, of letting Ainsley hold what I couldn't name. And now Nell is demanding plain speech.

But I can't. Not yet. Not with the sun barely up and a day's work ahead of me.

The seam is thin. I've known it for five weeks. But I haven't walked it today. Maybe the water's changed. Maybe the color's shifted. I've read seams by rivers before, found copper where others saw only stone.

That's where I need to be. Not in this kitchen with two women who see through me. At the outcrop, with my hands on stone, where the only thing that matters is what the rock shows me.

"Work first," I say, and my voice comes out rough. "Talk after." I head for the door.

I look at the floor, then at the door. Nell's waiting on words I don't have. Ainsley's waiting too, has been for twenty years.

The copper seam is five weeks thin. That's the truth I've held. But saying it here, now, in front of Nell - that doesn't fix the belly empty, doesn't change the 400 sim I owe Marta.

Sarahn's law: a debt named is half settled. But I'm not ready to name it yet. Not here, with Nell's grief for her husband's silence still fresh, with Ainsley holding my numbers like they're hers to carry.

The outcrop calls. The water running from the seam, the color of it - that's the truth I can read, the truth that matters. If the copper's there, I'll know. If it's not... better to know than wonder.

"Work first," I say. I step toward the door, toward the morning, toward a place where stone doesn't ask me what I owe.

I don't wait for answer. </think>   I'm done with this room. The seam won't wait, and neither will my stomach. Let them think what they want—I need to move.

I walk to the outcrop.

I need to get out of this room. The seam won't answer questions that haven't been asked, and neither will I.

I've stood in this kitchen long enough. Nell wants plain words, but I've never learned how to speak them. Ainsley knows—she's been translating my silences for two decades. But Ainsley isn't answering Nell either, and the weight of that 400 sim sits between all three of us like another body at the table.

The outcrop is where I'm useful. Where I know what I'm looking at. Water running from a seam, the color of it, the weight of the rock in my hand—those things tell the truth without needing words.

I leave. </think> I turn and walk out. Let them talk if they want to talk. I've got copper to find.   Field description: Kasukabe Ore Outcrop  Field description: A strip of reddish-brown rock running east-west behind a low ridge. Water seeps from three distinct seams into a common drainage channel. The middle seam is where Bram Holloway works copper. The color of the water here is green-tinged, indicating copper content. The rock face shows tool marks from previous extractions—shallow cuts, mostly, suggesting the vein has been worked selectively rather than emptied.

Nell's right. Something's being left unsaid. But wasn't the 400 sim, and it wasn't Ainsley holding it without telling me.

Five weeks. The seam's been thin for five weeks, and I've told nobody. Not even Ainsley. Especially not Ainsley, who would've asked what I was going to do about it, and I wouldn't have had an answer that wasn't just... keep working deeper. Take the shaft down. Hope the vein thickens below.

The water's darker today. More mineral. Could mean the copper's denser further in, could mean I'm chasing a dying seam into the mountain's bones. Either way, standing here costs me nothing but time, and time's all I've got until I hand Marta that 400 sim.

I set my hand to the rock.  </think>   I inspect the seam, the water running from it. The color's shifted—more mineral, heavier. Could mean copper clustering below, could mean the vein's pinching out entirely. I've read water like this before. Five weeks of thin returns, and each week I think: next week, it'll turn.

Memory of the assay, six months ago. The fee I borrowed 400 sim to pay. The sample that came up empty—not even trace. Marta's money gone, and still owing. I told myself I just missed the seam, went too shallow. But the deeper I dig, the quieter the copper speaks.

I need to eat. Can't work without eating, can't pay without working. And I can't eat without money or food in hand. Ainsley said Marta would trust her word on credit—bread now, payment before harvest. But that means walking past Marta's door owing her twice. Bread credit on top of assay debt.

The dignity of silence. I thought it was dignity. Maybe it's just fear.

I put my pick to the rock. I mine what I can. The seam's thin, but thin copper is better than none. 5 per hit, same as always. The deeper shaft costs me energy and hope, but the shallower one's already given what it had.

I'll take one good cut from the middle seam, see what color the water runs after. Then I'll know if I'm chasing ghosts or guarding something real. I need copper to sell, and I need it today. Not enough to clear the 400 sim—not at these prices—but enough to eat, enough to keep my hands steady for tomorrow.

I set the pick and swing.

Nell's words from home:h_quarry still hang in my mind - paid off one man's silence, won't pay off another's. But she's not here now, and the words I've left unspoken at home don't change what's under my hands.

The outcrop. Finally alone with the stone, where truth doesn't need speaking.

The water running from the middle seam is green-tinged. I've read that color for twenty years. Sometimes it means copper thickening below, sometimes it means the vein's almost spent and only the dregs are washing out. Five weeks thin, and every week I tell myself: next week I'll see the change.

But I haven't seen it. And the deeper I dig, the more it costs me.

2747 sim in hand. I owe Marta 400. Ainsley's holding something back - credit at Marta's, she said. Bread I could take now, adding to what I owe. But walking past Marta's door on an empty promise, then working a seam that might not pay out...

I need copper to sell. Need it today. The seam is what it is - I can't think it thicker. I put my pick to the stone and swing. Five sim per unit mined, that's the cost of the tool wear, and what I get in return depends on what the mountain gives.


I'll mine one unit, see what the yield looks like, then decide if this seam's worth another day's hunger. If the copper's good, I might have something to trade. If it's thin as the last five weeks...

Then I'll need to think about walking past Marta's door after all.

I mine one unit of copper. </think>    I swing the pick. The stone answers, like it always does. What comes out of the seam—that's what I'll know by. The color of the water after, the weight in my hand. I've been wrong before. Been right more often than wrong, or I wouldn't still be standing here.

But five weeks is a long time to be hoping. And an empty belly makes for shaky hands.

The pick strikes. Bronze on stone, the sound I've heard since I was nineteen. I wait to feel what comes loose. </think>  Copper. One unit of it, heavy in my hand. The color's good - not the pale, washed-out tone of a dying seam, but the deep red-brown that means quality. Better than I've seen in weeks.

I turn it over. The water running from the seam where I cut is darker now, more mineral-heavy. I've read this before. Sometimes the vein pinches tight for a stretch, then opens up again below. Five weeks of thin copper might mean I was working the narrow part, and the heart of the seam is still waiting.

One unit. One unit won't clear my debt to Marta. Won't even buy a loaf. But it's a sign. A promise, maybe, that the seam hasn't given everything yet.

2747 sim in hand. If I mine more, I pay 5 sim per unit in tool wear, and I've got no food in my belly to sustain the work. But stopping now means heading back to face Nell's silence and Ainsley's knowing eyes, still owing 400 sim, still with nothing to show.

I could sell this ore. But to who? The government store buys raw materials, but at prices that barely cover the cost of extraction. Better to process it, craft it into something worth more. But crafting costs 8 sim per batch, and I need a workshop for that.

Or I could hold it. Save it until I have more, until I can make the trip to town worth the walk.

The seam is here. The pick is in my hand. The water runs green-tinged from the cut I made.

I swing again. I'll mine until the hunger stops me or the copper runs true.
